演奏者通常站立於鑼後，手持兩根木槌；槌端纏橡膠，夾在相對的凸鈕之間，再以槌端敲擊: The player usually stands behind the gongs holding two wooden mallets; the tips are wound with rubber, and you slip a tip between opposing bosses and then strike a boss with it to sound the gong. A beginner should first learn the arrangement of the four gongs in pairs: for a right-handed player the low gongs are usually on the left and the high on the right, a formal ensemble uses all four, and some informal playing strikes only the three highest. For fast, loud playing an assistant can steady the gongs so that they do not sway.

甘丁甘鑼主要見於菲律賓馬京達瑙的庫林當合奏，作為次要旋律樂器；正式演出使用四鑼，: The gandingan is found mainly in the kulintang ensembles of the Maguindanao of the Philippines, as a secondary melodic instrument; formal performances use four gongs, while informal ones strike only the three highest, in signalling style and in competitive style. It can also be played solo, to imitate the tones of speech and to send messages over a distance, and at wedding contests two players take turns showing their skill while an assistant steadies the gongs.
甘丁甘鑼名稱語源不明，但見於馬京達瑙民間故事與史詩；《迪瓦塔卡薩利潘》中公主以鑼: The origin of the name gandingan is unknown, but it appears in Maguindanao folktales and epics; in Diwata Kasalipan a princess sends messages with gongs, which shows that this communicative use predates the Islamic period. The origin of the gongs is still disputed: the British explorer Thomas Forrest thought bossless gongs might come from China, and other sources say they came by way of Indonesia or Sarawak in Malaysia. Traditionally the gandingan is the secondary melodic instrument of the kulintang ensemble, and in the old way it was mostly played by women; later a competitive style of dense rhythms and the use of gongs to carry speech appeared. After the Second World War bronze was scarce, so steel plate, and later welded galvanised sheet, replaced it, and the timbre and size changed with the material.
甘丁甘鑼由四個大型、淺凸心、薄邊的懸掛鑼組成，音高可變但尺寸相近，依音高成對排列: The gandingan consists of four large hanging gongs with shallow bosses and thin rims, variable in pitch but alike in size, arranged in pairs by pitch, the lower usually on the player's left and the higher on the right, with intervals close to those of the four lowest kulintang gongs. The player stands and strikes the boss with a light, small wooden mallet wound with rubber; the newer welded galvanised-sheet ones are smaller and higher in pitch. A formal ensemble uses four gongs, and some informal playing uses only the three highest, which can imitate the tones of the Maguindanao language. The source does not say clearly how the volume is controlled. Compared with the agung, the mallets are lighter and smaller, the rims do not curl inward, and the gongs can be nested for carrying.
甘丁甘鑼的發聲體傳統以青銅製成，二戰後因青銅短缺，較常見以鋼板製作；近年則以鍍鋅: The sounding body of the gandingan was traditionally bronze; after the Second World War bronze was scarce and steel plate became commoner, and in recent years the boss, body and rim are made separately from galvanised sheet, welded and then ground into shape. The mallets are wooden, with rubber strip wound tightly round one end. The gongs may be hung from a branch or set in a sturdy wooden frame; the source does not state the materials of the other parts.
甘丁甘鑼（Gandingan）是菲律賓馬京達瑙族的一組四片大型懸掛鑼，屬11/1: The gandingan is a set of four large hanging gongs of the Maguindanao of the Philippines, belonging to the 11/12 system of tuned idiophones, gongs and bells, xylophones and lithophones. The faces are shallowly bossed and the rims thin; the gongs hang vertically from a branch or a wooden frame, arranged in pairs by pitch. The player stands and strikes the bosses with wooden mallets wound with rubber at both ends. It serves as the secondary melodic instrument in the kulintang ensemble, and can also be played solo to imitate speech, for communication, competitions and informal occasions.
